result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.is_arborescence()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Check if the graph is an arborescence (directed tree). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L9054-L9139){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.is_arborescence() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Is arborescence](/assets/graphs/is-arborescence.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: the six-node tree with every edge pointing away from the root A, so each other node has exactly one incoming edge and is_arborescence() returns True. Right: the same tree with the edge between C and F reversed (shown in the accent color); F now has no incoming edge, giving two roots, so is_arborescence() returns False." width="100%"} An arborescence is a directed graph which: - must be directed - has exactly one root (a node with in-degree `0`) - has other nodes with in-degree exactly `1` - must be weakly connected - has exactly `n - 1` edges This represents a tree structure with a clear parent-child hierarchy flowing from a single root. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if graph is an arborescence, `False` otherwise. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The in-degree pattern (one node with $\deg^-(v) = 0$ and every other with $\deg^-(v) = 1$) is what distinguishes an arborescence from other directed acyclic structures. Because each non-root node has exactly one incoming edge, every vertex has a *unique* directed path from the root, which is the property that makes arborescences the natural model for parse trees, dependency hierarchies, and dominator trees in compilers. The undirected analogue is `is_tree()`; in graph-theory literature this object is also called a directed rooted tree or an out-tree. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A directed tree growing outward from one root -- where every non-root node has exactly one incoming edge -- is an arborescence: ::: {#0a03315f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec arb = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["root", "A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("root", "A"), ("root", "B"), ("A", "C")]) ) arb.is_arborescence() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Two separate roots both pointing into the same node give it in-degree `2`, which violates the "exactly one incoming edge" rule: ::: {#140d0b98 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} multi_root = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["root1", "root2", "A"]) .add_edges([("root1", "A"), ("root2", "A")]) ) multi_root.is_arborescence() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` False ``` ::: ::: A directed cycle has no root at all, since every node has in-degree exactly `1`: ::: {#f8a148d7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} cycle = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) cycle.is_arborescence() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` False ``` ::: ::: Generated trees built with a single directed root, like `add_balanced_tree()`, are arborescences by construction: ::: {#986a1e04 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree = ec.Graph(directed=True) tree.add_balanced_tree(k=2, h=3) tree.is_arborescence() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: :::
